config.title: Build AST based code highlighter basics

intro.title: Build AST based code highlighter basics
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a basic code highlighter that uses an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) to analyze and color JavaScript code. You will learn how to parse code into an AST to understand its structure, then traverse this tree to identify different syntax elements like keywords, strings, and comments. The main technologies involved are JavaScript and a parser library to generate the AST. By the end, you'll have a working highlighter that applies different colors to code based on its syntactic role, giving you a hands-on introduction to ASTs and code analysis.
intro.usecase: AST-based code highlighters are essential in developer tools like VS Code's syntax highlighting, GitHub's code display, and Stack Overflow's code snippets. They power interactive coding playgrounds like CodePen and JSFiddle, where real-time syntax coloring helps developers write and debug code visually. These systems also enable intelligent IDE features like bracket matching, error highlighting, and semantic code navigation that professional developers rely on daily.

objectives: Construct a basic Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) parser to tokenize JavaScript code.
Apply token classification rules to categorize code elements such as keywords, strings, and numbers.
Implement a rendering function that converts classified tokens into styled HTML spans.
Configure a text input to serve as the source code for the highlighting system.
Initialize and update a display component to show the highlighted output in real-time.
Integrate the parsing, classification, and rendering steps into a single functional highlighter.
Manipulate the AST structure to handle nested code constructs like functions and loops.

steps.title: Parse the source code into an AST

steps.hint: Call acorn.parse() with the code parameter as the first argument. The parse method returns an AST object.
steps.expectedOutcome: The highlightCode function will now have an AST variable containing the parsed tree structure of the input JavaScript code.

steps.title: Define the node visitor function
steps.instruction: Inside the highlightCode function, define a function named 'visitor' that takes two parameters: 'node' and 'type'.
steps.hint: This function will be called for each node in the AST. Use a function declaration or arrow function.
steps.expectedOutcome: A visitor function is defined inside highlightCode, ready to process AST nodes.
successCriteria: The highlightCode function contains a 'visitor' function with 'node' and 'type' parameters.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Add string literal handling to visitor
steps.instruction: Inside the node visitor function, add a condition to check if the node type is 'StringLiteral'. When it is, push a span element with the string value into the result array.
steps.hint: Use an if statement to check node.type === 'StringLiteral'. Then use result.push() with a string like `${node.value}`.
steps.expectedOutcome: The visitor function will now detect string literals and wrap them in span tags for highlighting.
successCriteria: The visitor function contains an if statement that checks for 'StringLiteral' nodes and pushes a span element with the node's value into the result array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your condition checks node.type === 'StringLiteral' and pushes the correct span element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The visitor function doesn't yet handle string literals. Add an if statement for 'StringLiteral' nodes that pushes a span element.

steps.title: Add numeric literal handling to visitor
steps.instruction: Inside the visitor function, add an else-if condition to detect NumericLiteral nodes and wrap their value with a span tag with class 'number'.
steps.hint: Check if node.type equals 'NumericLiteral'. If it does, push a span element with class 'number' containing the node.value into the result array.
steps.expectedOutcome: The visitor function will now wrap numeric values (like 42 or 3.14) with <span class="number"> tags.
successCriteria: The visitor function includes an else-if condition for NumericLiteral nodes that pushes a span with class 'number' containing the node.value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're checking for 'NumericLiteral' type and pushing the correct HTML string with the node.value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The visitor function doesn't yet handle numeric literals. Add an else-if condition for node.type === 'NumericLiteral' that pushes a span with class 'number'.

steps.title: Traverse the AST with the visitor
steps.instruction: Inside the highlightCode function, after defining the visitor function, call acornWalk.simple() to traverse the AST using your visitor.
steps.hint: Use acornWalk.simple(ast, visitor) to walk through all nodes in the AST.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AST will be walked through completely, allowing the visitor to process each node.
successCriteria: acornWalk.simple() is called with the AST and visitor function as arguments.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling acornWalk.simple() with both the AST and your visitor function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The AST traversal isn't set up yet. You need to call acornWalk.simple(ast, visitor) to walk through the entire AST structure.

steps.expectedOutcome: The highlightCode function now returns a string of concatenated HTML span elements ready to be inserted into the DOM.
successCriteria: The highlightCode function returns the joined result array as a string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Return the complete highlighted code element
steps.instruction: In the highlightCode function, return the result array joined into a single string to create the final highlighted HTML output.
steps.hint: Use the join method on the result array to combine all the span elements into one string.
steps.expectedOutcome: The highlightCode function now returns the complete highlighted HTML string by joining all the span elements in the result array.
successCriteria: The highlightCode function returns result.join('') to produce the final highlighted code output.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
